narrative:
The model predicted an 84.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the middle of the class among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also worked against you, as you placed in the second decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth. Your LSAT score of 31 was the third biggest contributor; it sits noticeably below the 37-point average of those who were admitted and further increased the estimated risk of failing the bar.

None of these features alone doomed the application, but together they created a clear pattern the model associated with students who struggle to pass the bar on the first try. Your undergraduate GPA, family income bracket, and plan to attend full-time were much less influential.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. A higher class rank in future semesters and a stronger LSAT would directly address the factors that weighed most heavily against you.
